title: The Sallatha Sutta
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of accepting pain as it arises, rather than resisting or trying to escape it, in order to break free from patterns of suffering and ignorance. It highlights the difference between those who are untaught worldlings, who often respond with worry and resistance, and well-taught noble disciples, who can experience painful feelings without distraction and instead know how to transcend them through understanding and acceptance. By recognizing our tendency to be "fettered" by suffering, we can cultivate a deeper understanding and simply be present in the moment, without needing to change or achieve anything.

sentences.text: Announcements.
Thanks, Chris.
I thought this week, in this exploration of enlightenment, I'd dip into early Buddhism.
I want to explore a well-known sutta from the Pali Canon called the Sallatha Sutta.
Sutta is the Pali word for the Sanskrit sutra, so, early sutra.
Sallatha means a dart or an arrow.
The title points to the main metaphor of the teaching, which is that painful, difficult things in life hit us like an arrow, like a dart, and they hurt.
We all know that.
What the Buddha explores in this text is that awakened people may experience pain in a different way than ordinary people.
These early texts tend to be pretty wordy and repetitive and long to our ears, because we're impatient moderns with bad attention spans, I guess, is part of the problem.
But this one is nice and short, so it's very palatable, and we could pretty much read the whole thing.
This short sutra doesn't start out like they often do, describing where the Buddha was and who was present and bringing us into that moment back then.
It starts out with him speaking.
Here's the first paragraph, which describes the topic of the sutta.
*An untaught worldling, O Monks, experiences pleasant feelings.
He experiences painful feelings, and she experiences neutral feelings.
A well-taught noble disciple likewise experiences pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings.
Now what is the distinction, the diversity, and the difference that exists between a well-taught noble disciple and an untaught worldling?*
We're talking about two things right away.
One is the Buddhist mental factor of vedana, a feeling tone: the powerful, powerful way our mind tends to divide things into pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral.
And he's talking about two classes of people.
It's dualistic in a way.
One class is the untaught worldling, and the other class of people is the well-taught noble disciple.
I understand Kate did some exploration recently about this powerful mental factor, how it underlies so much of our suffering and so much of our potential for awakening.
It's such an important thing, and yet we tend to let it fly by as we easily elaborate in our minds on what's pleasant or unpleasant, with our opinions and our preferences.
Our mind is very good at justifying that.
It's like, "Of course I don't like such and such.
It sucks, blah, blah, blah."
But the Buddha suggests that we look more closely, always, right?
Here's the Buddha's deep dive into what really happens when we have a pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral feeling.
He especially emphasizes the unpleasant, painful things that happen.
Starting out with the untaught worldling, and I don't know if this is us or we're somewhere in between, you have to decide for yourself, here's what he says.
*When an untaught worldling is touched by a painful feeling, he worries and grieves.
She laments and beats her breast, weeps and is distraught.
He thus experiences two kinds of feelings, a bodily and a mental feeling.
It is as if a person was pierced by a dart and following the first piercing is hit by a second dart.
So that person will experience feelings caused by two darts.*
Ouch.
*It is similar with an untaught worldling.
When touched by a painful feeling, he worries, grieves, laments, beats his breast, weeps and is distraught.*
It seems a little repetitive.
Maybe I copied it wrong.
That's okay.
Two darts is the description here.
The first dart is being touched by something painful.
The text implies a physical experience as the first dart and a mental experience as the second dart, but we'll unpack that a little bit more in a minute.
And this is what happens with the untaught worldling.
I was getting up in the middle of the night to go to the bathroom last night, and I tried to go around the corner of the bed frame, as I've banged my toes there before.
But I failed.
I still banged my toe.
I felt the unpleasant feeling in my toe right away.
Ouch.
And I noticed it was immediately followed by an unpleasant mental feeling.
"Damn it.
I thought I had this down.
I was even trying to avoid it and I still hit it.
What a dope."
Ouch.
Which is small stuff really, right?
It wasn't that bad.
The discomfort lasted about a second and a half, and then maybe I added another couple of seconds beating myself up about it.
By the time I got to the bathroom, I was over it.
But small stuff can be a really good place to practice, because we can be so overwhelmed and confused and thrown by big stuff.
So I appreciated that I noticed the functioning of that teaching, and I was able to let go before getting to the lamenting, the breast beating and the weeping.
I didn't cry about this.
Modern interpreters suggest that the first dart, which is described in the text as a bodily feeling, could also be an emotional pain.
Somebody insults you.
You remember something awful.
We have so many ways that we have emotional pain.

As you know, I've been geeking out about neurology, and I remember reading that when they put people in the brain scanners and induce a physical pain, a little thing that heats up your finger until it really hurts, science, man, they notice some areas of the brain tend to be active.
Although now we know not to be too sure.
It's like one little piece of the brain, but some areas of the brain tend to be active when we feel a physical pain.
When we feel an emotional pain, and they can induce that with different stimuli, show you scary stuff on a picture or something, it's the same kind of reaction in the brain.
So someone insults you or something, that's painful, right?
But then we also are very good at adding a second emotional pain.
So this first dart, second dart thing can happen without a physical pain.
It can happen emotionally.
And I don't know that the Buddha made such a strong distinction between thoughts and emotions and physical sensations anyway.
It's all experience.
It was a different framework than we think of.

The implied practice point seems to be that maybe we don't have to throw that second dart, or the third dart or the fourth dart: beating ourselves up, blaming others, wishing it were some other way, resisting reality in all kinds of ways.
And accept that there is pain in life.
Maybe we can reduce it a little bit, but never completely, right?
Most of the time I actually do avoid the corner of the bed frame.
It's rare that I get it.
But that's small stuff, as I said, because right over the horizon, or maybe looming on the horizon, is the pain of sickness, old age, and death.
So is it possible to not have second darts about that?
Let's read on, though, because that's something that I, and a lot of people, are reading into this text, and I'm not sure he's actually saying that.
Here's what he says next, after talking about the untaught worldling being touched by a painful feeling, experiencing that, and then experiencing the second dart.
It's all about painful feeling to start.
He goes on and says, and by the way, this is all written with male pronouns.
I'll try to mix it up, but that's how it's written in this translation.
*Having been touched by that painful feeling, he resists it and resents it.
And in those who resist and resent that painful feeling, an underlying tendency of resistance against that painful feeling comes to underlie their mind.*
It gets really habituated.
An underlying tendency of resistance comes to underlie the mind.
*And under the impact of that painful feeling, she then proceeds to enjoy sensual happiness.
And why does he do so?
An untaught worldling, O Monks, does not know of any other escape from painful feelings except the enjoyment of sensual happiness.
And in she who enjoys sensual happiness, an underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feelings comes to underlie the mind.
Because she does not know, according to facts, the arising and endings of these feelings, nor the gratification, the danger, and the escape connected with these feelings.
And those who lack this knowledge, an underlying tendency to ignorance as to neutral feelings comes to underlie the mind.*
There's some deep conditioning we're doing here.
And I never noticed that before: an underlying tendency of ignorance as to neutral feelings that comes to underlie the mind.
*So that when you experience a pleasant feeling, a painful feeling, or a neutral feeling, you are fettered by it, chained up.
Such a one, O Monks, is called an untaught worldling who is fettered by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
She is fettered by suffering, this I declare.*
It gets pretty heavy, actually.
After having this multidart experience of pain, the ordinary person then compensates by trying to lose themselves in pleasure, says the Buddha.
Perhaps a little distraction and indulgence at one end of the spectrum, maybe all the way up to serious addiction at the other end.
Virtually seeking ways to distract, to overload, to numb, to avoid pain by seeking something that seems pleasurable.
The Buddha offers this analysis of why this might happen.
Let's read this again.
*Under the impact of that painful feeling, she then proceeds to enjoy sensual happiness.
And why does he do so?
An untaught worldling, O Monks, does not know of any other escape from painful feelings, except the enjoyment of sensual happiness.*
So it's out of ignorance, right?
It's always a root teaching in all of Buddhism.
It's out of not understanding the way things really are.
It seems like for the uninformed worldling, the only way out is to try to feel good.
Somehow I want to feel good again.
We can relate to this, I think.
Or at least, probably in our case, we do that, but we also at the same time kind of know better, right?
So maybe we're somewhere in between these two characterizations, but we'll get to the second characterization in a minute.
We're not completely ignorant, with all this practice, all these teachings.
And yet we still seem to be deeply conditioned in the way that he's talking about.
This next part is really such a powerful statement.
You start habitually trying to get sensual happiness to get out of this, and you get addicted.
An underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feelings comes to underlie the mind.
*And you do not know according to facts, the arising of these feelings, nor the ending nor the gratification, the danger, the escape connected with these feelings.*
There's something we need to learn about here, it seems.
Something about danger and escape.
And the part I had never noticed before, and I've read this a ton of times, so it's interesting, in a way they seem repetitive and simple.
Another way these early teachings have these little subtle elements that takes a lot of study, I think, to start to notice, and I'm sure I'm only just beginning here.
This point about the neutral feelings completely escaped my attention before.
When you get into this state of extra suffering and extra darts, when there's something unpleasant and you're reaching for the pleasant, you're just pulled back and forth like a yo-yo or something.
And you don't actually ever notice that plenty of experience is just neutral, neither painful nor pleasant.
That there's a peacefulness there, a possibility to take refuge in some way, a kind of ground of being.
The early Buddhist teachings emphasize that.
The goal is to calm down, settle into the peace that is the nature of reality.
He concludes the section reminding us that this is really quite a big deal.
It's not just, wouldn't it be nice to not beat yourself up when you bang into something?
It's an existential sort of threat to our ability to have a good life.
*That when you experience a pleasant feeling, a painful feeling or a neutral feeling, with the mind conditioned in this way, you're fettered by them all.
And so, O monks, is called an untaught worldling who is fettered by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
She is fettered by suffering, this I declare.*
This is why Buddhism has a bad reputation.
It seems so dire, but maybe we're a little in denial on it.
It really is quite dire, if we only live within our conditioned life, an endless hamster wheel of suffering.
We distract ourselves a little way, and most of us tend to be pretty privileged, so it's a gilded cage, you know.
But let's read on, because he's going to offer another vision here next.
He describes the alternative, the life of someone who's awakened to the real nature of it all, to the truth of the situation.
This is a much shorter passage, so I'll read the whole thing and we'll unpack it a little bit.
*But in the case of the well-taught, noble disciple, O monks, when she is touched by a painful feeling, he will not worry, nor grieve, nor lament.
She will not beat her breast and weep, nor will he be distraught.
It is one kind of feeling he experiences, a bodily one,* so the first dart, *but not a mental feeling,* the second dart.
*It's as if a person were pierced by a dart, but not hit by a second dart following the first one.
So this person experiences feeling caused by a single dart only.
It is similar with the well-taught, noble disciple.
When touched by a painful feeling, he will no longer grieve nor lament, will not beat her breast and weep, and will not be distraught.
He experiences a single feeling, a bodily one.* And apparently that doesn't bug him that much either.
It's just a feeling.
*And then, having been touched by that painful feeling,* and here [unclear: "Rick"] describes this, *having been touched by that painful feeling, he does not resist and resent it.* No resistance.
*Hence in her, no underlying tendency of resistance against the painful feeling comes to underlie the mind.
Under the impact of that painful feeling, she does not proceed to enjoy sensual happiness.
Why not?
As a well-taught, noble disciple, he knows of an escape from painful feelings other than by enjoying sensual happiness.
As a well-taught, noble disciple, he knows of an escape from painful feelings other than by enjoying sensual happiness.
Then, in him who does not proceed to enjoy sensual happiness, no underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feelings comes to underlie the mind.* All this conditioning isn't happening.
*And she knows, according to facts, the arising and ending of those feelings and the gratification, the danger and the escape connected with those feelings.
In she who knows thus, no underlying tendency to ignorance as to neutral feelings comes about either.
And when she experiences a pleasant feeling, a painful feeling, or a neutral feeling, she is one, he is one, who is not fettered by it.

Such a one, O monks, is called the well-taught, noble disciple, who is not fettered by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.* The noble, well-taught disciple is not fettered to suffering.
*This, I declare.*
And then pretty much he ends the talk.

What I noticed when I was trying to approach this fresh and say something about it, without realizing it at first, is that my mind always starts out with this sort of self-focused slant, a self-improvement slant.
How could I beat myself up less, you know?
How could I be a little happier?
And the Buddha is not really telling us how to do that here.
There are other texts, other angles on this, and other qualities of mind are described.
There's not so much a step-by-step guide.
There is another sutra called the Nissaraniya Sutta, which actually means the means to escape.
So I'm like, oh, good, maybe now he'll tell us.
How do we escape?
That sutta talks about six qualities.
I won't have time for the whole thing, and it doesn't really say how to practice or generate these either.
But there are six qualities that will help you escape, so it'd be good to know what those are, I think.
Here they are: goodwill, compassion, appreciation, equanimity, an understanding of the signless, which is kind of like emptiness, and letting go of self-identification in a very deep way.
So I thought, aha, maybe that's the root to all of this.
From the Buddha's deeper intention, approaching these teachings with "how could I suffer a little bit less?
How could I be better?" might not really be what he had in mind.
So let me just read you this one paragraph from the second sutta on the means of escape, about letting go of the self.
There's some powerful medicine here, I think.
Here's what the Buddha says.

*Furthermore, there is the case where a monk might say, "Although I am is gone, and I no longer assume I am this, still the arrow of uncertainty and perplexity keeps overpowering my mind."* So he's quoting a theoretical monk saying, *although I am is gone, and I do not assume I am this, still the arrow,* here's the arrow again, *of uncertainty and perplexity keeps overpowering my mind.* But the Buddha says, *no, don't say that.
Don't speak in that way.
Don't misrepresent the Blessed One.
The Blessed One would never say that.
It's impossible, because when I am is gone, and I am this is not assumed, the arrow of uncertainty and perplexity can never keep overpowering the mind.
That possibility does not exist, for this is escape.
This is escape from the arrow of uncertainty and perplexity, the uprooting of the conceit I am.*

So, well, maybe the Buddha on a deep level is not saying, in the Sallatha Sutta, the sutta about the two arrows, two darts, "Here's the problem, here's the direction you're going, so figure out a way to get from here to there."
Maybe you can stop throwing second darts at yourself.
That would probably help.
No, maybe he's saying something much more powerful about the nature of self.
And Dogen says this too, right?
To study the way is to study the self.
To study the self is to forget the self.
It's very famous, but how do we really practice that?
And then a little while ago we chanted the Heart Sutra, which reminded us of the same stuff.
It's not any of those things.
No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no.
Our illusion of self is so persistent, right?
So powerful.
So it brings me back to where I started.
Is there really anything wrong with suffering a little less?
No, you know.
So maybe it is just fine to work on this at two levels.
Sometimes we talk about the relative level and the absolute level.

At the relative level, I think we can interpret it that way: train yourself in noticing second darts, the ways we beat ourselves up, the ways we resist, and the ways we condition ourselves to try to escape through distraction and pleasures.
And could that turbulence in the mind make it so that we're not noticing ordinary everyday moments as neutral and grounded and simple, a moment of non-reactivity?
But I think it's good to go back to these source texts.
It seems like it's good for me anyway.
And remember that that's not the whole vision here.
That's incomplete.
I don't think there's anything wrong with it, but it's incomplete.
There's also a deeper vision.
In the sutra about the two arrows, he's saying that in the deeper vision, it's not that you notice and change course.
It's that you don't even perceive it that way.
You don't perceive a painful moment as painful in the way that we're thinking about painful.
Just experience, and experience.
And then there's another experience.
And you're not fettered.
You're not stuck.
You're not chained up.
In another sutra, which we don't have time for, he also talks about how this all makes sense if there are multiple lifetimes, sure.
And in a future lifetime, through this practice, you'll be happier.
He also says, and I didn't realize that he would talk this way, that if there are no multiple lifetimes, then even in this very life, you could be happier.
So that's also there.
So it makes me wonder about a big, light leap of faith and imagination.
It's maybe also a deep and important part of our practice to not get lost in little incremental improvements.
The other day we were talking, and Kate actually pointed out how in a lot of his recent stuff, Norman Fischer has been talking about the imagination.
So maybe that's why I'm talking about that.
But maybe a big part of our practice should be more to imagine in our gut, in our heart, not just our brain, a life free of suffering.
Imagine the life of the noble, well-taught one.
That could actually be possible, even though our relative mind can't actually conceive of it, because that's the nature of our relative mind.
And Zen is always trying to point in that direction, right?
With all these stories of awakening, the finger pointing to the moon and so on and so forth.
So I land back at the end here on the kind of both-and case, which I think is best, at least that's my opinion.

We could really hold both, but we need to not forget either end of this spectrum: that we can train ourselves day by day in being wiser about how we meet pleasant, painful, and neutral, but we can also imagine, breathe, and sit, and dream in the possibility of not being caught at all by painful, pleasant, or neutral.
Not needing to navigate better, not needing to be more aware, because it's just so clear.
It's just so obvious.
It's just how it is.
There's no need to try hard.
There's no need to do anything other than be.
To try to put this into some kind of tangible format, I thought I'd share a little contemplative exercise to close, and then maybe we can talk about whatever you notice.
I'm borrowing an exercise from a mindfulness class in self-compassion.

Their orientation is a little different than this, but I think this exercise gets at what I'm trying to say: if we compare in this exercise different ways that we respond to suffering, we may be in a way encouraged that we already do have within us an unfettered kind of freedom in responding to suffering.
And we have definitely within us a very fettered, conditioned way of responding to suffering.
I don't want to give away the punchline of the exercise, so I invite you to give yourself a little stretch if that's helpful.
We've been sitting here a little while.
Take a deep breath.
This might be a good one to close your eyes and feel into your felt sense and breath and body for a moment.
Platform for all deep contemplation.
And I want to invite you to bring to mind a memory.
We're going to use this imagination here a certain way.
Bring to mind a memory of a time when someone you know and care about was suffering and you were supportive.
You were part of the support system.
I'll give you a minute to just let that bubble out of your consciousness or your unconscious anyway.
Think of a specific time when there was someone you care about who was suffering and you were able to help.
You were a support.
And once you think of an incident like that, really bring it back to mind and feel into what it was like to be in that situation with this person, however it was formally arranged.
And think about how you were in that situation.
How did you support your friend?
What kind of language did you use?
What was your tone?
What were you like if you had to describe yourself from afar?
What kind of person were you in supporting your friend or relation through their suffering?
So you saw suffering here and you responded in a certain way.
Now let's let that example go.
I want to invite you to think of a second life example.
Think of a time when you yourself were suffering.
A particularly potent example might be a time you made a mistake, screwed something up, and there was suffering.
You accidentally caused harm or just at least created confusion or trouble.
So think of a particular time when that happened.
These are often not too hard to think of.
And then think especially of the moment you noticed, that kind of oh moment.
And what do you remember of how you responded to yourself?
There's a voice in you that talks to you when something goes sideways.
How did that voice talk to you?
What kind of words did you use talking to yourself about this time of suffering or stress or mistake or something?
What was your tone of voice with yourself?
What was your attitude?
How would you describe that part of you that was responding to your own suffering?
What kind of person is that in there?
And that's probably enough of that.
Let's let that go.
Maybe a sigh or a little shoulder roll is nice there.
Just taking a little moment and just sitting, breathing.
Stop the recording.
